description: I am looking for enthusiastic teammates with skills in coding, web development, designing, research, and creative thinking to build an innovative project together.
summary:
Since the 1960s, NASA has left machines on the Moon, on Mars, and in deep space. Many finished their work long ago, but their stories are not well known.
Our project is a website that tells these stories to school-age space fans, in simple English and with NASA pictures.
The Home page has two big buttons: Moon Missions and Mars Missions. We wrote 13 mission pages:
Mars (9): Sojourner Rover, Spirit & Opportunity, Viking Landers, Phoenix & InSight Landers, Dawn, NEAR Shoemaker, Pioneer 10 & 11, Ingenuity Helicopter, and Kepler Space Telescope.
Moon (4): Apollo Lunar Modules, Lunar Roving Vehicles, ALSEP Science Packages, and Surveyor Landers.
We used a dark space background with warm orange colors. The website works on phones and computers, and we built it with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.
details:
1. What does it do, and how does it work?

Our project is a website called “Space Archeology: The Story We Left Behind.” It tells the stories of NASA machines that were left on the Moon and Mars, like rovers, landers, and space probes.

On the Home page, a visitor chooses Moon Missions or Mars Missions. Each choice opens a page with mission cards. When the visitor clicks a card, a full story page opens. In total there are 13 stories. Each story has key facts, a timeline, NASA pictures, the science the machine did, and its legacy. There is also a Team page.

The website is one HTML file. When you click a button or a menu option, JavaScript shows the right page. The page does not reload, so it is fast.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • It explains difficult space missions in simple words, so young students can understand them.
  • It puts many missions in one place, with pictures and timelines.
  • It is free and easy to use. It opens in any browser, on a phone or a computer.
  • It teaches students about space history and science.

3. What is the intended impact?

We want school-age space fans to see that old space machines still matter. They are abandoned, but not forgotten. We hope the stories make young people curious about space and science, and help them learn about the science each machine made possible.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Languages: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.
  • Software: a code editor and a web browser. We also used an AI assistant (Claude by Anthropic) to help us write and fix the code. (Please keep this line if it is true for your team. Many competitions ask you to say when you use AI.)
  • Content and pictures: NASA websites and the NASA image library, and Wikimedia for some Moon pictures.
  • Hardware: our own laptops and phones. (Change this if you used something else.)

5. How is the project creative?

  • We used the idea of “space archeology.” We treat old space machines like ancient places that tell a story.
  • The design has a dark space background with warm orange colors, so it feels like old machines resting in space.
  • Big photo buttons and photo cards make the website feel like a museum.
  • Every mission page has its own look, but all of them keep the same color style.

6. What factors did your team consider?

  • Our audience: school-age students, so we used simple words and short paragraphs.
  • Correct facts: we used NASA information for dates, numbers, and names.
  • Easy to use: a clear menu, big buttons, and “Back” buttons on every page.
  • All devices: the website works on phones, tablets, and computers.
  • Reading comfort: a dark background with light text, and a dark shade over photos so the words are easy to read.
  • Teamwork: we shared the 13 missions among the team and joined them into one website.
